743.title: Paula and Eustochium
743.hook: a Roman widow and her daughter who studied Hebrew and worked with Jerome
743.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Paula and Saint Eustochium as saints, and Jerome's letters to and about them are among the main sources for their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ignorance of scripture is ignorance of Christ. Your line was know the book, know him. Which line from the Gospel page stayed with you? Day seven hundred forty-three.

Jerome wrote a long letter about a mother after she died, and one scene in it is hard to read. A small boy on the shore stretches out his hands toward her, and his sister silently begs her to wait. The ship is ready to sail east. The mother is Paula, a wealthy Roman widow. Beside her on deck is her daughter Eustochium. Jerome says Paula lifted her eyes to heaven and didn't look back at the shore. Jerome doesn't pretend it was easy; he says it tore at her. She was leaving a whole life behind for Bethlehem.
screen: `A BOY ON THE SHORE.` → `A SHIP READY TO SAIL.` → `PAULA SAILS FOR BETHLEHEM.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. Paula came from the Roman nobility. Eustochium was one of her daughters. Both had studied scripture in Rome in a circle of women Jerome taught, before any of them left. Second, the language. In Bethlehem, Jerome says, Paula set out to learn Hebrew, so she could sing the psalms in the language they were written in. And he says she managed it, and Eustochium too. These weren't patrons who simply paid for a scholar's work. They were students of the text, reading it in the original alongside him. Third, the questions. Jerome says Paula made him read through the scriptures with her. And when he hit a passage he couldn't explain, and honestly said so, she wouldn't let it go. She'd press him with fresh questions until he told her which meaning he thought most likely. A student like that makes a teacher better. Fourth, what they built. In Bethlehem, Paula founded communities for women living a life of prayer, and a place to welcome pilgrims. Jerome dedicated works to them, and after Paula died he wrote her long epitaph as a letter to Eustochium. He says she died with verses of the psalms on her lips, the psalms she had worked so hard to learn. So Jerome's Bible didn't come from a scholar working alone. In Bethlehem he worked alongside two women of the book who wouldn't stop asking.
screen: `A ROMAN WIDOW AND HER DAUGHTER.` · `THEY LEARNED HEBREW.` · `SHE WOULDN'T LET A QUESTION GO.` · `A TEAM IN BETHLEHEM.` · then, large: `WOMEN OF THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a woman scholar. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who knows something deeply and wouldn't let you read it carelessly. Someone who pressed you with a question you couldn't answer yet, or sat with you over a hard page. Remember one moment with her. Hold it for a while. Then decide how you'll thank her: a message, a note, a call. If she's gone, or out of reach, you can simply say her name. If you pray, you can thank God for her. The bell holds the time.
Paula and Eustochium. A Roman widow and her daughter who learned Hebrew in Bethlehem and read the scriptures with Jerome. Today's word.
Your line: women of the book. Today, send the thank-you you just planned. One sentence is enough. Day seven hundred forty-three.

744.title: John Chrysostom (c. 347–407)
744.hook: the golden-mouthed preacher: honor Christ in the poor before you gild his altar
744.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint John Chrysostom as a Doctor of the Church, and his words on honoring Christ in the poor are read in the Church's Office of Readings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paula and Eustochium, women of the book who learned Hebrew and kept pressing Jerome with questions. Did you send your thank-you? Day seven hundred forty-four.

Silk hangings. Gold cups on the altar. And outside, someone with no clothes, in the cold. Those pictures sit side by side in one of John's sermons on Matthew, and he puts them there to make his listeners uncomfortable. Tradition remembers him by a nickname, Chrysostom, golden-mouthed, for his preaching. But the golden mouth wasn't always sweet. Today he asks his wealthy listeners a question about where they keep their gold, and who they think they're honoring with it.
screen: `SILK AND GOLD INSIDE.` → `SOMEONE COLD OUTSIDE.` → `THE GOLDEN MOUTH SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: First, the question, from one of his sermons on Matthew. Do you want to honor the body of Christ? Then don't ignore him when he is naked. Don't honor him here in church with silk, while outside you neglect him, cold and without clothes. Second, why he can say that. He's leaning on Jesus's own words in Matthew, the same words Sulpicius tied to Martin's cloak. In the Douay-Rheims: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Chrysostom puts two sayings side by side. The one who said, this is my body, he points out, is the same one who said, I was hungry and you gave me no food. If Christ is present at the altar, he's also at the door. Third, the order. What good is it, he asks, to load Christ's table with gold cups while he himself is dying of hunger? Feed him first, he says. Then adorn his table too. Fourth, what he isn't saying. He doesn't call beautiful churches a sin. He says plainly he isn't forbidding gifts for the altar. He's asking for the poor alongside them, and before them. Gold cups and a fed neighbor can belong together. The danger is gold instead of the neighbor. He later served as bishop of Constantinople, made powerful enemies there, and died in exile. The golden mouth wasn't always a safe one.
screen: `DO YOU WANT TO HONOR HIS BODY?` · `YOU DID IT TO ME.` · `FEED HIM FIRST.` · `NOT GOLD INSTEAD OF THE POOR.` · then, large: `HONOR HIM IN THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give before you decorate. Settle, and breathe. Think about the next thing you're planning to spend money on just to make something nicer. A new phone case. A candle. A plant for the shelf. Nothing wrong with any of it. Now, before that, choose one gift to someone in need. A food bank, a shelter's wish list, a meal for the person who sits outside the store. It can be small. Settle on what, and when. Then picture the nice thing after it, in its place. If you pray, you can ask to see Christ in the person you're giving to. The bell holds the time.
John Chrysostom. The golden-mouthed preacher who said to honor Christ in the poor before you gild his altar. Today's word.
Your line: honor him in the poor. Today, make the gift you chose before you buy the nicer thing. Day seven hundred forty-four.

745.title: The Easter homily
745.hook: his short Easter sermon, still read at Orthodox Easter: come, the first and the last
745.howItsDone: In Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic churches the Paschal homily attributed to John Chrysostom is read aloud at the Easter night service, and some Latin-rite Catholics read it during the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Chrysostom, the golden mouth: honor him in the poor before you gild his altar. Did the gift come before the nicer thing? Day seven hundred forty-five.

Past midnight, deep into the Easter night service. Candles everywhere, people standing shoulder to shoulder, some of them worn out from the long fast, some of them who didn't fast at all and just walked in off the street. Then the priest reads a short sermon. Orthodox churches, and Eastern Catholic churches of the same Byzantine tradition, read it on Easter night. Tradition gives it to John Chrysostom. And it speaks straight to the person at the back who feels they don't belong here tonight.
screen: `EASTER NIGHT, PAST MIDNIGHT.` → `THE FASTERS AND THE LATECOMERS.` → `ONE SHORT SERMON.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome. The sermon opens by calling in everyone who loves God to enjoy this bright feast. Then it starts counting the hours, and you realize where you are. It's the parable of the workers in the vineyard, from Matthew. Some started at dawn. Some at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth. Some came at the eleventh hour, with barely any day left. Second, the surprise. In Jesus's parable, the landowner pays everyone the same, and the early workers grumble. The homily takes that story and turns it into an invitation. If you came at the eleventh hour, it says, don't be afraid because you're late. The Master is generous. He receives the last just as the first. He welcomes the deed, and honors even the intention. Third, the table. You who fasted and you who did not, the homily says, rejoice today. The table is full. Let no one go away hungry. Nobody is checking who earned a seat. Fourth, why. Because of what Easter is. The homily ends by turning to death itself, using Paul's words. In the Douay-Rheims: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" Christ is risen, it says, and life reigns. So in the homily the generosity isn't a mood. It comes from the empty tomb: if death has lost, there's no reason to turn latecomers away. The eleventh hour, too, gets the full wage.
screen: `COUNTING THE HOURS.` · `THE LAST, JUST AS THE FIRST.` · `THE TABLE IS FULL.` · `DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?` · then, large: `THE ELEVENTH HOUR TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite someone who came late. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's arrived late to something you're part of. The new person on the team. The cousin who missed years of family dinners. The neighbor who just moved in. Someone who came back to church after a long time away. Hold their face for a moment. Then think of one small way to say, the table is full, there's room for you. An invitation to lunch. Saving them a seat. Introducing them to someone. If you pray, you can thank God for the ones who welcomed you when you were late. The bell holds the time.
The Easter homily. The short sermon tradition gives to John Chrysostom, read at Easter in Byzantine churches: the last are welcomed just as the first. Today's word.
Your line: the eleventh hour too. Today, make the invitation you just thought of, to the person who came late. Day seven hundred forty-five.

746.title: Patrick's Confession
746.hook: Patrick's own words begin: I, Patrick, a sinner
746.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Patrick's feast day, and some read his Confession, or the prayer known as his Breastplate, which tradition attributes to him, on that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Easter homily: the last received just as the first. Your line was the eleventh hour too. Who did you make room for? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Ego Patricius peccator rusticissimus. I, Patrick, a sinner, very unlearned. Those are the first words of a short document in rough Latin, written by the man himself, in what he calls his old age. It doesn't begin with a miracle, or a boast, or a list of churches founded. It's a man telling the truth about himself, and giving thanks. Today we read from Patrick's own account, the one he called his confession.
screen: `I, PATRICK, A SINNER.` → `A SHORT BOOK IN ROUGH LATIN.` → `THE TRUTH ABOUT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, where he starts. Patrick names his father, a deacon, and his grandfather, a priest. He grew up in a Christian family in Britain. And then, he says plainly, he didn't know God. Raiders seized him from his father's estate and carried him off to Ireland, a captive. He doesn't dress it up. He says he deserved to be taken, because he and the others had turned away from God. Second, what happened in captivity. He was put to tending flocks, out in the cold, the snow, the rain. And there, he says, the love of God grew in him. He prayed many times in the day and again in the night. The place of his slavery became the place he met God. Third, the voice. One night, he says, he heard in his sleep that his ship was ready. He ran, crossed a long distance, and found a ship, and after hardships came home. A few years later, back with his family, he had a dream. A man came from Ireland carrying letters, and Patrick read the heading of one: the voice of the Irish. He heard them calling him to come and walk among them again. He went back, to the land where he'd been a slave. Fourth, why it opens with sinner. Patrick wrote the confession, he says, to give thanks, and to answer people who doubted him. He's embarrassed by his Latin, and says so more than once. He doesn't make himself the hero. In his telling, the story belongs to God, who found a boy in a field. The man telling it starts with the truth about himself.
screen: `A DEACON'S SON WHO DIDN'T KNOW GOD.` · `A SLAVE IN THE FIELDS, PRAYING.` · `THE VOICE OF THE IRISH.` · `HE STARTS WITH THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `I, A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one honest sentence about yourself. Settle, and breathe. Get a scrap of paper, or open a note on your phone. Patrick started with his name and the plain truth. Try the same: your first name, and one true thing you'd usually leave out of the story. Not a punishment. Not a speech. Just honest. I, Sam, have been short with people I love this week. I, Ana, am more scared than I let on. Write it, then read it back once without arguing with it. If you pray, you can hand that sentence to God, the way Patrick handed over his. The bell holds the time.
Patrick's Confession. His own short account, in rough Latin, that begins: I, Patrick, a sinner. Today's word.
Your line: I, a sinner. Today, keep your honest sentence somewhere you'll see it, and see whether it changes the way you speak about others. Day seven hundred forty-six.

747.title: Brigid of Kildare
747.hook: abbess and legend-maker; her cross is woven from rushes
747.howItsDone: Catholics in Ireland and beyond keep the feast of Saint Brigid, and some families weave a Brigid's cross from rushes or straw to hang over a door or in the kitchen through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patrick's Confession, a book that opens with a man calling himself a sinner. Your line was I, a sinner. What honest sentence did you write about yourself? Day seven hundred forty-seven.

A handful of green rushes, pulled from a riverbank. Fold one over another, turn, fold again, turn, and a small square grows in the middle with four arms reaching out. Tie the ends with a bit of thread. In Ireland people still make these, and hang them over the door or in the kitchen, where they stay until the next one replaces them. It's called Brigid's cross. The woman it's named for ran a great double community of nuns and monks in Ireland, and so many stories gathered around her that it's hard to see where the woman ends and the legend begins. Today, Brigid.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF RUSHES.` → `OVER THE DOOR.` → `BRIGID'S CROSS.`

segments.voice: Start with an early life of her, written by a monk of Kildare named Cogitosus. He says plainly that he's writing down what he heard from older people. So from the first page, we're in the land of memory, not records. Cogitosus tells of a woman whose hands were always open. She gave food and clothing away so often that, in his telling, what she gave kept coming back: butter that didn't run out, milk that stretched to feed more guests than it should have. One story is pure delight. Coming in from the rain, she hung her wet cloak on a beam of sunlight, mistaking it for a wooden beam, and the cloak hung there, drying, as if on a peg. Next, the work. Cogitosus describes Kildare as a large community where both women and men lived under her care, with a church where they prayed, and people coming from all over for help. An abbess is the woman who leads a community of nuns. Brigid led one so well that it became a place people traveled toward. Now the cross. The rush cross isn't in Cogitosus. It comes from a later story people tell: Brigid sitting beside a dying man who did not know Christ, picking up rushes from the floor, and weaving a cross while she told him who Jesus was. In the story, he asks to be baptized before he dies. Some tellings make the man her father, some a chieftain. Whatever happened by that bed, the cross outlived it. Rushes are about the plainest thing a person could pick up: free, damp, growing at the water's edge. That's why the story sticks. She didn't need a jeweler or a carpenter. She used what was on the floor. Catholics honor Brigid as a saint, one of Ireland's patrons alongside Patrick, and on her feast people still weave her cross with their hands.
screen: `AN OLD LIFE, FROM MEMORY.` · `HANDS ALWAYS OPEN.` · `THE ABBESS OF KILDARE.` · `A CROSS FROM THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `A CROSS FROM RUSHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a small cross from anything. Look around where you are. Two pens. Two twigs. A pair of paper strips torn from a receipt. Two blades of grass. Lay one across the other. You don't need rushes or a pattern. Hold it in your palm. Notice how little it took. Then sit quietly with it for the time the bell gives you. If you pray, you can hold it while you pray for someone in your home, the way people do when they hang Brigid's cross by the door. If you don't, simply notice what you made from what was lying around. The bell holds the time.
Brigid of Kildare. Abbess of a great community in Ireland, honored as a saint, remembered for open hands and for the cross woven from rushes. Today's word.

Your line: a cross from rushes. Today, put the little cross you made somewhere you'll see it, a doorway, a desk, a pocket, and let it remind you that small, plain things can carry a lot. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

748.title: Leo meets Attila (452)
748.hook: the bishop of Rome goes out to meet the invader, and Attila turns back
748.howItsDone: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Pope Saint Leo the Great, honoring him as a Doctor of the Church, and his meeting with Attila is told as part of his story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brigid of Kildare, the abbess with open hands. Your line was a cross from rushes. Where did you put the little cross you made? Day seven hundred forty-eight.

An army is loose in northern Italy. Attila, king of the Huns, has come down into Italy, and cities are falling behind him. In Rome, the emperor's court has no good answer. Nobody knows whether Rome is next. And so a small group sets out north, toward the army, not away from it. Two high officials of the empire. And with them, the bishop of Rome, a man named Leo, the pope. No soldiers to speak of. Just a delegation walking toward the invader himself. Today, what happened when they met.
screen: `AN ARMY IN ITALY.` → `A SMALL GROUP GOES NORTH.` → `THE BISHOP OF ROME.`

segments.voice: The account we lean on comes from Prosper of Aquitaine, a writer of Leo's own time who kept a chronicle. It's short, and it's careful. Prosper says the emperor, the senate and the Roman people looked for a plan, and none seemed better than sending envoys to the savage king to ask for peace. So Leo went, trusting in God's help, Prosper says, with the two officials beside him. Next, the meeting. Prosper says Attila received the envoys well, and was so pleased by the presence of the high priest that he ordered the fighting to stop. He promised peace and went back beyond the Danube. That's it. No speech is recorded. No threats, no miracles. A bishop walked out, met a conqueror, and the conqueror turned around. Now, the legends. Later centuries weren't satisfied with something so quiet. A later story says that as Leo spoke, the apostles Peter and Paul appeared above him with swords drawn, and Attila took fright. Prosper says nothing of it. Some readers also note that other writers of the time mention hunger and sickness in Attila's army, which may have helped him decide. We don't know everything that was in Attila's mind. We only know what Leo did. And here's the line worth keeping: he went out. When everyone else was asking how to keep the danger away, Leo walked toward it. Catholics remember him as Saint Leo the Great, a pope and a teacher of the Church. It wasn't a battle he won. It was a meeting he showed up to.
screen: `PROSPER'S SHORT ACCOUNT.` · `ATTILA RECEIVES THEM.` · `THE LEGEND ADDS SWORDS.` · then, large: `HE WENT OUT.` · then: `A MEETING HE SHOWED UP TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to face a hard meeting calmly. Bring to mind one conversation you've been avoiding. A call to return. A talk with someone you love. A meeting at work. Don't solve it. Just let yourself walk toward it in your mind, the way Leo walked north. Breathe slowly. Notice where your body tightens, the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, and let that place soften a little on each breath out. Picture yourself sitting down across from the other person, steady, listening first. If you pray, you can ask God for calm before that meeting. The bell holds the time.
Leo meets Attila. The bishop of Rome walks out to the invader, and the invader promises peace and turns back. Today's word.
Your line: he went out. Today, take one step toward the conversation you thought about: send the first message, or set the time. Day seven hundred forty-eight.

749.title: Christian, recognize your dignity
749.howItsDone: Catholics hear Leo's Christmas sermon in the Office of Readings at Christmas, and the Catechism opens its section on life in Christ with his line about recognizing one's dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo meets Attila: the bishop of Rome walking north toward an army. Your line was he went out. Did you take one step toward that hard conversation? Day seven hundred forty-nine.

Same man, different day. Not on a road facing an invader this time, but in a church in Rome, on Christmas, preaching to a crowd. This sermon starts with joy: our Savior is born today, he tells them, so let us be glad, because there's no room for sadness on the birthday of Life. And then, partway through, he turns and speaks to each listener directly, as if pointing at them. Christian, recognize your dignity. The line has traveled a long way. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it today. Today's word is the one he called them by: Christian.
screen: `CHRISTMAS IN ROME.` → `NO ROOM FOR SADNESS.` → `HE SPEAKS TO EACH ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with what comes before the line. Leo has been preaching that in the birth of Jesus, God took on our human nature, so that people could share in God's own life. That's the whole engine of the sermon. Then comes the turn: Christian, recognize your dignity, and since you've been made a sharer in the divine nature, don't go back to your old meanness by the way you live. Next, the reminder. Leo tells them to remember whose body they belong to, and who its head is. Remember, he says, that you were rescued from the power of darkness and brought into God's light and kingdom. Notice what he's doing. He doesn't say: you are worthless, so try harder. He says the opposite. You have been given something enormous, so live like someone who has it. The dignity comes first. The living follows from it. The Catechism places this line at the opening of its section on the Christian life. Before it talks about any commandment, it reminds the reader who they are. Now the word itself. In the Acts of the Apostles, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch. For Leo's listeners, it was a name that tied them to Christ. When he calls out Christian, he isn't scolding a crowd. He's naming them. And a little look back at this week. Paula and Eustochium learning the book. Chrysostom honoring Christ in the poor. The Easter homily welcoming the eleventh hour. Patrick calling himself a sinner. Brigid with open hands. Leo going out. And today, Leo again, telling people their worth before telling them anything else.
screen: `GOD TOOK ON OUR NATURE.` · `RECOGNIZE YOUR DIGNITY.` · `WORTH FIRST, THEN LIVING.` · `A NAME TIED TO CHRIST.` · then, large: `KNOW YOUR DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat yourself with dignity today. Sit as if you were worth sitting well. Feet flat. Back long. Shoulders down. Breathe slowly. Now notice the voice in your head that talks to you through the day, the one that comments on your mistakes. Listen for its tone. Then try saying one thing to yourself the way you'd speak to someone you respect. Plainly, kindly, without flattery. If you pray, you can hear Leo's line as spoken to you: Christian, recognize your dignity. If you don't, simply rest in the posture of someone who matters. The bell holds the time.
Christian. A follower of Christ, the name the disciples were first called at Antioch, and the name Leo used to call his listeners to their dignity. Today's word.
Your line: know your dignity. Today, do one ordinary thing with care, as if you were worth the care: eat sitting down, dress with attention, or rest when you need to. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
